lines.text: Keep a steady pace. A squad that sprints the first hour walks the rest.
Eyes on the treeline, not your feet. The road will still be there.
Count the milestones. If we're lost, I want to know how lost.
Talk if you like, but quietly. Voices carry further out here.
We'll rest at the next stream. Fill your canteens there, not before.
Are we nearly there? Don't laugh, I'm only asking once.
I've never been this far from the village. The trees even smell different.
Race you to that big rock? No? Fine. Later.
I packed six rice balls. Six. Want one?
Does the road look like the map to you? Because it doesn't to me.
That hill there? My grandfather farmed it before the road was paved.
You ninja walk so quietly. It's unnerving, honestly.
I make this trip every season. Never with company before.
There's a tea house at the crossroads. Best roasted chestnuts this side of the river.
Do they teach you to carry that much without complaining? I'm impressed.
Watches in pairs, two hours each. Wake the next pair, don't just nudge them.
Small fire, low smoke. We're guests in these woods.
Eat, then sleep. Tomorrow's a long road.
Good work today. I mean that. Now get some rest.
Sit a while. Tell me something you learned today that the Academy didn't teach you.
Can you see all those stars? There's never this many over the village.
I can't sleep. Want to talk for a bit?
Do you think we're doing well? On this mission, I mean.
If you snore, I'm putting a leaf in your mouth.
This is the first time I've slept outside. It's not so bad, with the squad here.
Thank you for the fire. And the company. I don't usually have either on the road.
I brought dried persimmons. Here, take a handful. Go on.
My family thinks I'm mad, travelling with goods at my age. Maybe I am.
You lot sleep in shifts? Then I'll sleep soundly. First time in years.
Tell me about the Leaf. I only ever see the market.
We're here. Stay together and let me do the talking.
Good. On time and in one piece. That's a mission done right.
Look around. Remember this place. You'll be back one day.
Rest tonight. We report in the morning.
Well done, all of you. That road was longer than it looked.
We made it! We really made it!
It's so different from home! Look at the roofs!
Can we get something to eat first? Please?
I'm writing this down. First town I've ever been to.
My legs have turned to jelly. Worth it, though.
Here we are. I'd thought the trip would be worse. Much worse.
My shop's just past the well. Come in, have some tea before you go.
I'll be telling everyone the Leaf's ninja are the best on the road.
Thank you for seeing me home. Truly.
Ha! Not one bandit. You must have frightened them off just by walking.
Down! Protect the client!
Ambush. Positions, now. Nobody chases them into the trees.
Stay calm. Remember your drills. Guard the cart.
Form up behind me. Watch the sides, not just the front.
They want the goods, not a fight. Let's make sure they get neither.
They're in the trees! Everyone, look out!
I'll cover the client! Go!
Bandits! Real ones! Okay. Okay. I can do this.
Back to back! Like we practised!
I knew that bird call sounded wrong!
Bandits! I knew it! I knew it!
Not the cart! Please, not the cart!
Do something! That's what I'm paying you for!
I'll stay under the wagon, if that's all right with everyone.
Oh, spare me! I'm only a poor merchant!
Good. Check for injuries, then check the cart.
That's how it's done. Calm, together, no one left behind.
You did well. All of you. I'll say so in the report.
Tie them and leave them for the border patrol. We keep moving.
Breathe. It's over. Drink some water.
We won! Did you see me? Did you see?
My hands won't stop shaking. Is that normal?
Good teamwork! Really good. High five!
We did it without anyone getting hurt. That's the best part.
I'm starving now. Fighting makes you hungry.
Remarkable! I've never seen anything like it!
You're worth every ryo. Every single one.
My heart's still pounding. Thank you, thank you.
I'll be adding a bonus to your pay. Don't argue.
And you're just Genin? Imagine the Jonin!
C-rank, escort. {client} travels to {place} and wants a squad alongside. Two days' walk. {pay}.
Escort duty for {client}, as far as {place}. Bandits have been seen on that road. Stay sharp. {pay}.
Your squad's first escort? {client} to {place}, door to door. Keep the client comfortable and alive to complain. {pay}.
I'm bound for {place} with my wares. I've heard stories about that road. I'd like some ninja with me.
You're my escort? You look young. No offence. The last escort was all beard and no sense.
Just see me to {place} in one piece. And my cart. Mostly my cart.
Good. We leave at dawn from the main gate. Don't be late.
Excellent. I walk slowly and complain often. You've been warned.
Right then. I'll pack an extra rice ball for each of you.
No? I'll wait for another squad. I'm not walking that road alone.
Pity. I'll hire someone from the next village, if I live that long.
Hm. Fine. The Mission Desk will find me someone braver.
How much further? My feet are writing letters of complaint.
Did you hear that? In the trees? No? Just a bird? Good.
We've made good time. At this pace, {place} by tomorrow evening.
{place}! At last! I owe you a fine meal, all of you.
Not a scratch on me or the cart. You're welcome to escort me any time.
We're here. I didn't think we'd make it so smoothly. Tell the Leaf I said so.
I'll walk the rest myself. You've been more trouble than the road.
My cart's in a ditch and my wares are in a river. Some escort.
We turned back? After all that? I'll want words with your Mission Desk.
Escort to {place}, complete. {client} wrote a letter. A long letter. Mostly good.
Logged. Your first road out of the village and back. How was it?
Good work. Escorts are the backbone of C-rank. Quiet, long, and worth every ryo.
C-rank. {count} bandits are holding the road near {place}. {client} wants them gone. Drive them off or bring them in. {pay}.
Bandit trouble at {place}. Thieves, not shinobi, as far as we know. {count} of them. Careful anyway. {pay}.
{client} has lost three carts this month near {place}. Clear the bandits, bring back what you can. {pay}.
They come out of the trees at {place}. {count}, maybe more. They took my whole harvest.
We can't take our goods to market. Nobody can. Not with those bandits on the road.
I'm not asking you to hurt them. Just make them leave. And maybe bring back my rice.
Thank you. The bend by the twin pines is where they hide.
Bring back what you can. Even half the rice would carry us through winter.
Good. Be careful. They're cowards, but cowards in a crowd are bold.
Then the road stays closed, and the market goes hungry.
I see. I'll ask the Desk to post it again.
No one wants to face them. I don't blame you, but I hoped.
Did you find their camp? Are they still there?
They say one of them has a club the size of a log. Mind that one.
Fewer on the road this week. Something's working.
The road's open! We'll be at market by the weekend!
You brought back my rice! And my cart! And... my neighbour's goat?
No more bandits. I'll sleep tonight for the first time in a month.
They're still out there. Worse, they're angry now.
You let them go? All of them? With my rice?
The road's no safer than it was. I'll wait for a stronger squad.
Bandits cleared from {place}. Those you brought in are with the police. Well done.
Logged. {client} sent a sack of rice to the Desk. We're keeping it.
Good. Remember this one: you won without hurting more than you had to. That's the job.
Long-distance delivery: {item} to {target}, all the way to {place}. Four days there and back. {pay}.
C-rank courier work. {client} needs {item} in {target}'s hands at {place}. Sealed. Don't open it. {pay}.
A far run for {client}: {place}, past the river crossing. The parcel is {item}. Pack for rain. {pay}.
This {item} has to reach {target} in {place}. It can't go with the merchants. Too many hands.
I'd go myself, but my knees and that road don't get along. Please, {place}, and quickly.
Give it to {target} and no one else. If {target} isn't there, bring it home.
Good. Here. Keep it dry and keep it close.
Thank you. {target} will know it's from me by the knot.
Safe travels. And bring back news of {place}, if you can.
It's a long way, I know. I'll find someone.
Then it waits. Some things are worth waiting for.
No? Hm. The Desk will have another squad soon.
Is it still sealed? Good. Good.
How far to {place} now? Two more days, maybe less.
Rest at the inn by the ford. They know the Leaf there.
All the way from the Leaf? For me? Thank {client} for me. Thank you, too.
It's here, and it's sealed. You've no idea what this means.
{target} has it. I can stop worrying now. Thank you.
It's opened. The seal's broken. This is no use to anyone now.
You lost it? On the road? Where on the road?
Too late. {target} left {place} two days ago.
Delivery to {place}, confirmed. A thank-you letter came back by hawk this morning.
Logged. Long road, that one. You've earned a bath and a hot meal.
Good. Courier work across the border is how the Leaf keeps its friends. Remember that.
D-rank, lost pet. {client} hasn't seen {target} since yesterday. Last sighting near {place}. Pays {pay}.
A pet search for {client}. The animal answers to {target}, apparently. Try {place} first. {pay} on return.
{client} is offering {pay} for {target}, safe and sound. Bring a treat and patience. Mostly patience.
You're the one from the Mission Desk? Thank goodness. {target} slipped out the back gate and never came home.
{target} always goes to {place} when there's a storm coming. Please, I've looked everywhere else.
It's {target}. My {target}. Small, scruffy, bites when frightened. Don't take it personally.
You'll really look? Here, take this. It's {target}'s favourite dried fish.
Thank you. Call the name softly, it hates shouting.
Bless you. I'll leave the gate open and the bowl full.
Oh. Of course. You must be busy with real missions.
Never mind. I'll keep walking the streets myself.
I understand. If you see {target} anyway, just... tell me?
Any sign? Even a paw print?
Someone saw something small and scruffy by {place}. Could be.
Don't grab at it. Crouch down and let it come to you.
{target}! You're home! Look at you, all burrs and mud!
You found {target}! I could cry. I might cry. Thank you.
There's my troublemaker. Thank you, truly. Go and claim your pay.
Look, it remembers me! Thank you for bringing {target} back.
Still nothing? I suppose that's it, then.
Maybe {target} found a new home. I hope it's a kind one.
Thank you for trying. Really. It's not your fault.
Pet returned. {client} sent a note. Most of it is just the word "thank you".
Another lost animal home. Logged. Wash your hands, would you?
Done, then. You'd be amazed how many of these we get. Pay's at the counter.
Weeding at {place}. {count} rows, by hand. {client} is paying {pay}. Bring gloves.
D-rank for {client}: clear the weeds from {place} before they choke the beans. {pay}.
Garden work at {place}. Not glamorous, but every Genin does it. {pay}.
The weeds have taken {place} over. {count} beds of them. My back won't let me bend any more.
Pull them up by the root, mind, or they're back in a week. All {count} rows.
Not the little purple ones! Those are herbs. Everything else goes.
Wonderful. The basket's by the shed. Fill it as many times as you need.
Good. Start at the far end, by the fence. It's worst there.
Thank you. I'll bring you barley tea at noon.
Fine. The weeds and I will keep arguing on our own.
No one wants the weeding. I know. I know.
Pity. My knees were counting on you.
That's the way. Get the roots, not just the tops.
You're faster than the last Genin. Much less complaining, too.
Half done already? Have a drink. It's hot work.
Look at that! I can see the soil again!
Every row clear. My vegetables thank you, and so do I.
Lovely work. Not a dandelion left standing.
You pulled up the radishes. All of them. Every single one.
Half the beds are still green. I'll finish myself, I suppose.
That's not weeding, that's just stepping on things.
Weeding done. {client} says you can come back any spring.
Logged. There's dirt on the report form. There's always dirt on these.
Good. Garden missions build patience. Your sensei will tell you the same.
Delivery. {client} needs {item} taken to {target} at {place}. Don't drop it. {pay}.
Simple run: {item}, from {client} to {target}. {place}. Back by evening. {pay}.
D-rank courier work. {item} for {target}. {client} says it's fragile, so it's fragile.
This {item} has to reach {target} at {place} today. It can't wait.
Take it straight there, no detours, and put it in {target}'s hands. Nobody else's.
It's {item}. Careful, it's heavier than it looks. {target} at {place} is expecting it.
Perfect. Here. Hold it with both hands.
Thank you. Tell {target} I said hello.
Good. Off you go, and don't run on the bridge with it.
No? I'll ask the courier, then. Slower, but they'll go.
Ah. I suppose I'll carry it myself, slowly.
All right. Someone else will take it.
Not delivered yet? {target} will be wondering.
You still have it? Good. Keep it out of the rain.
{place} is that way, past the noodle stand. You can't miss it.
Ah, the {item}! Right on time. {client} always sends the good ones.
Delivered and in one piece. Thank you. Tell {client} it arrived.
That's mine? Wonderful. Here, I'll sign for it.
It's broken. You brought me a broken {item}.
Too late. The day I needed it has come and gone.
That's not even mine. Did you mix up the parcels?
Delivery confirmed. {target} signed for it. Good, clear handwriting for once.
Logged. Three more of these on the board, if your legs are up for it.
Done. Most of the village's post goes through Genin, you know. Not much glory, plenty of trust.
Babysitting for {client}. {count} hours with {target}. Bring a book. Bring two. {pay}.
{client} has an errand across the village. Watch {target} till they're back. {pay}.
Childminding, D-rank. {target} is, I'm told, "a bit lively". Read that how you like. {pay}.
I'll only be {count} hours. {target} is no trouble. Mostly no trouble.
Bedtime is after supper. No sweets. Fine, one sweet. One!
{target} has been begging to meet a real ninja. Please don't do anything too exciting.
Thank you! Snacks are on the shelf. The high one.
Oh, you're a lifesaver. Don't let {target} near the paints.
Good. If anything happens, the neighbour across the way knows what to do.
Oh dear. I'll have to take {target} with me, then.
I don't blame you. I'd run too.
No? That's all right. Grandma can probably manage. Probably.
Is everything all right? It's very quiet. Quiet is suspicious.
You've lasted an hour! That's a record.
Did {target} eat anything that wasn't food? Just checking.
You're both still smiling! What's your secret?
{target} says you're the best ninja in the whole village. High praise.
The house is standing and everyone's fed. Thank you, really.
Why is the cat painted blue?
{target} is on the roof. How is {target} on the roof?
I came home to tears. Everyone's, by the look of it.
Babysitting complete. You look more tired than after a C-rank. They always do.
{client} has already asked for you again. That's a compliment, or a warning.
Logged. Sit down a moment before the next one. Children are harder than bandits.
Repairs at {place}. {client}'s {item} needs fixing before the next rain. {pay}.
D-rank handiwork for {client}: {count} boards on the {item} at {place}. Tools provided. {pay}.
{client} needs help mending the {item}. Hammer, nails, honest work. {pay}.
The storm took half the {item}. I've got the wood, I just haven't got the hands.
{count} boards, all rotten through. Pull them, replace them, done. Easy for a ninja.
Mind the old nails. Some of them have been in that {item} longer than I've been alive.
Good. Hammer's in the bucket. Watch your thumbs.
Thank you. Start with the corner; it leans worst.
Fine, fine. Measure twice before you cut, mind.
Then the {item} can fall down a bit more. It's good at that.
I'll ask a Kinoshita carpenter. Expensive, but they'll come.
All right. I'll prop it with a broom and hope.
Straight! Keep it straight! Look along the edge.
That's sounding good. Steady knocks, not angry ones.
How many left? Don't skip any, I'll be counting.
Look at that. Sturdier than it was new.
It doesn't wobble! It's never not wobbled!
Fine work. You could do this for a living, if the ninja business ever dries up.
It's crooked. It's very crooked. It's worse than before.
You nailed the door shut. From the outside.
I'll have to call a carpenter to fix your fixing.
Repair done, {client} says. Also says you hammer like a woodpecker. Fondly, I think.
Logged. Half the village's fences have a Genin's nails in them somewhere.
Good. The Kinoshita carpenters will grumble you're taking their work. Ignore them.
Target Practice, Youngest Year
An Academy teacher, {client}, needs extra hands for the youngest year's target practice in {yard}. {pay}.
Thirty first-years and one of me. Set the targets in {yard}, then walk the line and fix their grips.
Mind their elbows, not their aim. Aim comes later. Bad elbows last forever.
Wonderful. The little ones will be thrilled. Try not to look too impressive, they'll copy everything.
Good. Bring patience. Somebody always throws backwards on the first day.
That's all right. I'll split them into two halves and lose my voice instead.
Pity. They were hoping for a real Genin. I'll tell them you're on something secret.
Fingers along the flat, not around the ring. Show the one at the end, would you?
Halfway down the line. Nobody's hit a window yet. That's a record.
Every target hit at least once and every kunai back in the box. You'll have fans now.
Did you see their faces? Half of them want to be you. Thank you, truly.
Let's call the class early. Too many kunai in the wrong places for my liking.
Not today's lesson, then. Children learn from a bad day too. So do teachers.
Academy assist, done. {client} wrote "they listened". From that teacher, that's a medal.
Target practice signed off. Any first-years follow you here? Check your pack.
That target dropped before the kunai even touched it. Someone's sawn through the cords.
Three targets rigged to fall. One of the older years thinks this is very funny.
The whole class is chanting for a real combo. They won't throw another kunai until they see one.
"Show us! Show us!" Well. One clean three-hit combo, then back to grips.
Four practice kunai sailed clean over the wall. They're numbered. They have to come back.
Tutor Wanted Before the Test
A parent wants a tutor for {client}, an Academy pupil, before the next test. Study sessions at {library}. {pay}.
{client} reads the scroll and nothing stays in. The test is in three days. I'm at my wits' end.
Sit with {client} in {library} a few afternoons. Someone who passed recently might explain it better than I can.
Thank you. {client} is shy at first. Give it a day before you judge.
Bless you. I'll pack two lunches for the library. Big ones.
Oh. I'll try the older pupils, then. Someone must have a free afternoon.
I understand. I'll keep drilling the hand signs at supper. We'll manage.
{client} said you made the chakra chapter sound simple. That's never happened before.
Still struggling with the history dates? So did I. So did everyone.
A pass! {client} ran the whole way home waving the paper. Thank you.
{client} wants to keep studying with you. Wants to! I don't know what you did.
A fail, but closer than last time. We'll try again next term.
{client} cried, then said "next time". That's something. Thank you for trying.
Tutoring, complete. The parent says {client} is a different child. Nice work.
Signed off. The Academy staff asked who the tutor was. I may have bragged on your behalf.
{client} isn't slow at all. {bully} takes that lunch every day, and nobody can study hungry.
The test was never the trouble. It's {bully}, by the gate, every noon.
Something's tucked in {client}'s sleeve. A cheat sheet, written very small and very neatly.
Take the cheat sheet off {client} before the quiz, or let it go and say nothing?
A cheat sheet in the sleeve. Confiscate it, or look the other way just this once?
Bath House: Scrub and Stoke
{client} at {bath} needs the tiles scrubbed and the fires stoked before the evening rush. {pay}.
Tiles first, brush in circles. Then the fire under the big tub, and keep it high till dusk.
The boiler's in back at {boiler}. Feed it slow. A greedy fire just smokes.
Good. Sleeves up, sandals off. You'll be the cleanest Genin in the Leaf by six.
Excellent. There's a free soak in it after, if you finish before the regulars come.
Back to scrubbing alone, then. My knees send their regrets.
No? The regulars will complain the water's cold. They always do anyway.
Those corner tiles. Look at the grout. Do it again.
Water's starting to steam. Keep the wood coming, steady.
Tiles shining, water perfect. The regulars will think I hired a team.
Feel that steam. That's a proper bath. Thank you.
Cold water and a dirty floor at opening time. I'll be giving refunds all night.
We'll open late. People will grumble. Go on, I'll finish up.
Bath house job signed off. You smell of cedar smoke. That's how I know it was done right.
{client} says the boiler hasn't burned that evenly in years. Logged, and paid.
The boiler won't catch. Damp wood, cold flue. A fire or wind technique would get it going.
A regular dropped a locker key in the big bath. Somewhere on the bottom, under all that steam.
Night Watch at the Kiln
The kiln family wants a squad overnight at {kiln}. Fetch wood from {woodlot}, keep the heat even till dawn. {pay}.
A whole season's pots are in that kiln. The fire can't drop, not for one hour, until dawn.
Split wood from {woodlot}, stacked by the mouth. Watch the colour of the flame. Orange is too cold.
Good. I'll make tea. A lot of tea. It's a long night.
Thank you. Sleep this afternoon if you can. You won't tonight.
Then I'll sit up alone again. My eyes will close at three. They always do.
No matter. We'll wait for a drier week and a bigger squad.
Bright yellow at the spyhole. Good. Another armful in an hour.
Midnight. The worst part. Talk to me so neither of us dozes off.
Dawn, and not one pot lost. Hear that ringing when I tap it? That's a good firing.
Look at that glaze. You helped make that. I'll save you a cup from this batch.
The heat dropped too long. Half the shelf came out cloudy. We'll fire again.
A bad firing. It happens to every potter, even my grandmother. Go home and sleep.
Kiln firing, done. You're grey with ash. Go and wash before you sit on my chairs.
{client} sent a little cup with the report. Says it's for the squad, not for me. Fine.
A sharp crack from inside the kiln. One pot's split. Some shelf is sitting too near the flame.
Rain, right on the kiln roof. Grab the tarp corners and hold it till the cloud passes.
Mind the Children, One Afternoon
{client} needs someone to mind the children at {home} this afternoon. Feed them, count them, keep them inside. {pay}.
Lunch is on the shelf, naps after. If they ask for sweets, the answer is one each and only one.
Count them every so often. There should always be the same number. You'd be surprised.
Thank you! They've been asking for a real ninja all week. Brace yourself.
Wonderful. The little one bites when overtired. Not hard. Mostly.
Oh dear. I'll take them to work with me and hope nobody notices.
No? Their grandmother will have to come. She'll spoil them rotten.
Are they still alive? And the furniture? Good, good.
They told the neighbour you're teaching them a secret jutsu. Are you?
Fed, washed and asleep? Before supper? Are you sure you're a Genin and not a miracle?
The children want to know when you're coming back. Every one of them asked.
Paint on the walls and nobody napped. Well. They're in one piece. That's the main thing.
I think they won this round. Children usually do. Thank you for trying.
Childcare, done. You've got jam in your hair, did you know? Logged anyway.
{client} says the children haven't stopped talking about you. You're an afternoon legend now.
The youngest won hide-and-seek half an hour ago and still hasn't come out. The others are scared now.
Everyone's found but one. The little one hides too well. Check {hiding} before anyone starts crying.
Nobody's settling until they see a real jutsu. A clone would do. Two clones and they'd faint.
One of them is burning up. Medicine from {hospital}, quick, but you can't leave the others alone.
Deer Count, Nara Forest
The Nara clan wants help counting deer in {forest}. Quiet feet only. {client} will meet you at the fence. {pay}.
We count the herd every season. Walk slow through {forest}, tally the does, the bucks and the fawns.
They know our clan's smell. Yours, not yet. Stay downwind and don't chase anything.
Good. Here's the tally board. Don't drop it, they'll eat it.
Fine. Bring rice crackers. The deer will find you either way, they might as well like you.
Hm. The deer won't mind. My mother will. I'll count them myself, slowly.
That's all right. The herd will still be here next season. Probably bigger.
Count the fawns twice. They hide behind their mothers and spoil the numbers.
That old stag with the split ear? Don't count that one again. It wanders.
A herd that size, and healthy. The elders will be pleased. Quietly, but pleased.
Your tally matches mine within two. That's good for a first count. Very good.
Too much noise. Half the herd's gone deep into the trees. We'll try another morning.
The count's no good like this. Never mind. The deer keep their own time.
Deer count, delivered to the Nara. Here's the tally. You've got a hoofprint on your sandal.
Done. The Nara don't hand out compliments, but {client} said "adequate". That's practically praise.
A fawn caught in the brambles, and the doe won't let anyone close. Slow, low, and talk softly.
The clan's medicine-makers want every antler shed this season. They'll be lying in the bracken.
Tend the Aburame Gardens
The Aburame keepers are on duty and need someone to tend {garden}. Water the beds, touch nothing that moves. {pay}.
Water the beds at {garden} at the marked hours. The insects know their work. Yours is the plants.
If something lands on you, stand still. It is only curious. So are you.
Good. The beetles prefer calm visitors. Breathe slowly.
Thank you. Wear long sleeves. Not for safety. For your comfort.
Understood. Most people decline. The garden will wait.
Very well. I will ask a cousin to come home early.
The moths are resting on the left bed. Water around them, not on them.
You've stopped flinching. They notice that.
Every bed watered and every colony content. You have a gentle hand.
The garden is calmer than when I left it. That is the best thing I can say.
The beds are dry and the hives are restless. We will set it right. Thank you for coming.
Not a good day for the garden. It recovers. So will you.
Insect garden, done. Is that a beetle on your collar? No? Good. Signed off.
{client} said you were "quiet in the right way". From the Aburame, that's warm.
The lid on this box is open and the colony's gone walkabout. Rare beetles, all over the paths.
One flower here opens only after dark, and someone has to watch it happen and write it down.
Blocked Drain, Before the Flood
The drain at {drain} is blocked and the street floods with every rain. {client} is paying {pay}. Bring a bucket.
Water's up to my doorstep every time it rains. Something's choking {drain}. Leaves, muck, who knows.
Dig it out before tonight's rain, please. My floor mats can't take another soaking.
Thank you. There's a rake by the wall. Don't ask what's on it.
Good. I'll put the kettle on. You'll want a hot drink after that.
Then I'll sandbag the door again. My back loves that.
No? Fine. I'll just keep my sandals on the top shelf.
Is that the bottom yet? It smells like the bottom.
Water's moving! Just a trickle, but it's moving.
Listen to it gurgle. That's the best sound I've heard all month.
Clear! The whole street owes you. I'll make sure they know.
Still blocked, and here comes the rain. Up on the step, everyone.
Never mind. It's been blocked for years. One more night won't kill me.
Drain cleared. Please stand over there while I log it. Further. Thank you.
Drain job, done. {client} says the street stayed dry last night. Pay's waiting.
Something glints in the muck. A ring. {client} lost one down here last spring, didn't they?
The drain's full of frogs. Dozens. A whole frog kingdom, and they'll need moving to the river.
Careful with that rake! There are frogs everywhere. They'll have to go to the river in buckets.
The ring's in your palm. Give it back to {client}, or pocket it? Nobody would ever know.
Clear the Lot for a Training Post
{client} wants {lot} cleared for a new training post. Weeds, stones, an old woodpile. {pay}.
That lot at {lot} has been a jungle for ten years. Clear it to bare earth and we'll raise posts next week.
Stones to the wall, weeds to the heap, anything rusty to me. Don't just kick it into a corner.
Good. Gloves are by the gate. Wear them. There's bramble in there with teeth.
Right. Start at the road and work in. That way you can see how far you've come.
No? The weeds will be taller than you by summer. Your loss.
Hm. I'll wait for a bigger squad. It's a big lot.
You've found the old path! I forgot that was there.
Half bare already. Don't slow down now.
Bare earth, flat and clean. The carpenters can start on the posts tomorrow.
Look at that. Ten years of bramble, gone in an afternoon. Good work.
We'll leave it for now. It's been wild this long. It'll keep.
Not finished, but the road side's clearer. That's something.
Lot cleared. They'll name the new post after someone important, not you. Sorry. Paid, though.
{client} says it's the tidiest lot in the district. Logged.
Stop. There's a tripwire under these weeds, still taut. An old training trap, and it's still armed.
That buzzing is the woodpile. Hornets. A lot of hornets. They've claimed it.
Timber Haul for the Kinoshita Yard
The Kinoshita yard needs timber hauled from {woodlot} to {yard}. Heavy work. Good pay: {pay}.
Cedar, cut and seasoned at {woodlot}. Bring it to {yard} on the sledges, stack it bark side up.
Lift with your legs. A carpenter with a bad back is a carpenter with a short career.
Good. The sledge ropes are new, so no excuses.
Excellent. My apprentices will be glad of the help, even if they won't say so.
Fine. The logs aren't going anywhere. They're logs.
No? Then the new house frames will just wait another week.
Stack those flush. A crooked stack is a falling stack.
That's half the woodlot. Have some water before the next run.
A full stack by sundown. The yard hasn't looked this good since the spring rush.
Good timber, well stacked. My family will build something fine with it.
Not enough for the frames, but we'll piece it together. Go home and rest your arms.
Half a stack. We'll finish it ourselves. Thank you anyway.
Timber haul, done. You've got sawdust in your ears. Very carpenter of you.
{client} says the stack's straight enough to build on. From the Kinoshita, that's praise.
The stack's slipping! Three logs loose and rolling straight for the river!
An apprentice is down, foot under a log. Get them to the hospital first. The timber can wait.
Barbecue House: Party Order
The kitchen at {kitchen} has a party of forty tonight and not enough hands. {client} is asking for a squad. {pay}.
Forty guests, twelve grills, one kitchen. Slice, skewer, carry. Ask before you touch the marinade.
Pork belly thin, onions thick, and no tasting off the board. Well. A little tasting.
Good! Aprons on the hook. You'll eat well tonight, I promise you that.
Perfect. Wash your hands, then wash them again. My kitchen, my rules.
More grilling for me, then. I'll survive. I always survive with a full plate.
No? Shame. There was a staff dinner in it.
Table four wants more short rib. Table four always wants more short rib.
You're fast with that knife. Don't get cocky, keep your fingers tucked.
Forty guests fed and every plate came back clean. Sit. Eat. You've earned it.
That was a beautiful service. My father would have cried. He cries at good service.
Burnt meat and cold rice. They'll forgive us. Our regulars always do. Mostly.
A rough night. Every kitchen has them. Come back hungry some time and I'll feed you properly.
Kitchen help, done. You smell like the barbecue house. I'm now very hungry. Thanks for that.
{client} sent a note and a box of leftovers. The note's for the file. The box is for you.
The house spice tin's empty. Mid-service! Run to {grocer} before the next table comes in.
The chef wants an honest opinion of the new sauce. It tastes like burnt plums and regret.
The chef's waiting, spoon in hand. Tell the truth about that sauce, or be polite and say it's lovely?
Hot Lunch to the Training Ground
A catering order from {kitchen} for {ground}. It has to arrive hot. {client} is paying {pay}.
Twelve boxes for the squads at {ground}. Rice, grilled fish, pickles. Hot when it leaves, hot when it lands.
Carry them flat and don't stop to chat. Cold fish is a crime in this kitchen.
Good! The boxes are stacked by the door. Go, go, go.
Thank you. Mind the lids. They pop off if you run too bouncy.
Then I'll run it myself and burn the next batch. Wonderful.
No? I'll find a faster pair of legs. No offence.
Still steaming? Good. Keep going.
Don't take the market road at noon. You'll never get through.
They said it was still hot! Hot! You must have flown.
Every box delivered and not a grain spilled. You can carry for me any day.
Cold fish and soggy rice. They ate it, but they weren't happy. Next time, then.
Late and cold. I'll send a free dessert to apologise. Not your fault entirely.
Catering, delivered. The squads at the training ground say thank you through full mouths.
Done. {client} says it arrived hot. That's all anyone wants from a catering run.
{genin} is blocking the path, offering to "inspect" the food first. With chopsticks already out.
A box just tipped down the stairs. Run back to {kitchen} for another before the rest goes cold!
Parcels Before Sundown
A sack of parcels needs delivering across the village before sundown. {client} at the porters' office has the list. {pay}.
Three parcels: {a}, {b} and {c}. Names are on the labels. Get a thumbprint for each.
Before sundown, mind. After that people lock up and pretend they're out.
Good. Here's the sack. Heavier than it looks, isn't it?
Right. Don't open anything, don't shake anything, don't sit on anything.
More legwork for me. My feet thank you not at all.
No? The parcels will wait. The people waiting for them won't be pleased.
One down? Good. The next street's quicker by the canal path.
Still a few to go, and the sun's dropping. Hurry a little.
Every parcel delivered and every thumbprint taken. That's a clean sheet.
All before sundown. You'd make a good porter, if the shinobi thing doesn't work out.
Undelivered parcels, back in my sack. I'll be hearing about this tomorrow.
Not everyone got their parcel today. Never mind. Tomorrow's another round.
Delivery run, done. Thumbprints all here. One's a pawprint. I'll allow it.
{client} confirms all parcels in. Logged. Your sandals look tired.
These two labels are swapped. {a}'s parcel has {b}'s name on it, and the other way round.
Nobody lives here any more. The house is empty. Maybe {gossip} next door knows where they went.
This one rattles. Something breakable inside. Walking pace, and no roof-hopping with it.
Sealed Letters, Noon Bell
Sealed letters from the Residence to {o1}, {o2} and {o3}, all before the noon bell. {pay}.
Three letters, three offices: {o1}, {o2}, {o3}. Hand them over in person. Not to a doorstep.
The seals stay unbroken. If one cracks, you come straight back here. No excuses.
Good. The bell rings at noon whether you're done or not.
Right. Satchel's on the hook. Signed for, all three.
Fine. I'll send one of the runners. They're slower, but they're here.
No? Then the offices will wait. They're used to it.
One delivered? Good. Don't stop for dango on the way.
The bell tower says half past eleven. Move.
All three, signed and sealed, before the bell. Exactly how it's meant to go.
Clean work. The offices didn't even have time to complain.
The bell's rung and one letter's still in the bag. That office will be furious.
Too late for noon. I'll have to send an apology with it now.
Messenger run, logged. All seals intact. You'd be amazed how rare that is.
Letters delivered. The receipts are in order. {client} is quietly delighted.
{o2} won't let you leave. They're writing a reply right now and you're to carry it back.
Another squad's got the very same letters! Whoever reaches the offices first gets the credit.
Errands for an Elder
{client} needs some shopping done. {shop1} and {shop2}, then home with the bags. Short and kind work. {pay}.
Here's my list. Rice, miso and pickled plums from {shop1}. A tin of the green tea from {shop2}.
Not the cheap tea. The one in the blue tin. They'll try to sell you the cheap one.
Lovely. Take my purse. Count the change, mind. They know my eyes aren't good.
Thank you, dear. My legs don't do the market stairs like they used to.
That's all right. I'll go myself tomorrow. Slowly.
Busy, are you? Young people always are. Off you go, then.
Did you find the blue tin? It's on the top shelf, behind the counter.
Back already with half? Good. The rest can wait while you sit a minute.
Everything on the list, and the right tea! You're a treasure.
All here, and the change counted. You're more careful than my grandchildren.
Not quite everything. Never mind. I'll make do. I've made do for eighty years.
The wrong tea, and no plums. Still, you came. That counts.
Errands, done. {client} called you "a good child of the Leaf". Logged, with a smile.
Elder errands, signed off. You've a rice cracker in your pocket. Gift, I assume.
"Oh, and soap. And a new broom. And did I say lamp oil?" The list keeps growing.
The tea's poured and the cushion's ready. There's a story of the old days coming, and it won't be short.
Weed the Field Before Planting
{client} needs {field} weeded outside the wall before the planting. Sun hat recommended. {pay}.
Every row in {field}, roots and all. Leave a root and it's back in a week, laughing at us.
Bindweed's the worst. Thin and pale, wraps round everything. Pull it slow so it doesn't snap.
Good. Hoe's in the shed. Start where the scarecrow is and work out.
Thank you. I'll bring barley tea at noon. You'll want it.
No? The weeds will win, then. They usually do.
I'll do it myself, row by row. My back will curse your name.
You've got the knack. Fist low, twist, pull.
Halfway. Drink something. The sun's at its worst now.
Clean rows from wall to ditch. We'll plant tomorrow. Thank you.
Not a weed left. You've given this field a proper start.
Half the rows done. It'll have to be enough. Seeds don't wait.
The weeds won this time. I'll plant around them and hope.
Farm weeding, done. You've a sunburnt nose. Wear the hat next time. Logged.
{client} says the field's ready to plant. That's a farmer's whole year in a sentence.
The crows are back. One's sitting on the scarecrow's hat, eating the seed.
Fresh boar tracks right across the rows. Big ones. The desk at {desk} will want to hear about this.
Metal under the soil. An old cloth bundle of kunai, buried in the rows years ago.
A buried cache of kunai, rusty but sound. Turn it in at the desk, or keep it?
Festival Setup, Main Street
The festival committee wants lanterns hung and stalls raised on {street}. {client} is in charge. {pay}.
Stall frames first, then the lantern strings. Everything's in {store}. Red lanterns on the left, white on the right.
Don't let anyone talk you into "just one more string". There's always one more string.
Splendid! You'll see your own lanterns lit tonight. That's the best part.
Good. Mallets and rope at {store}. Bring a friend if you have one spare.
No? I'll rope in the committee. They'll complain about their knees.
Ah. Well, someone has to be the crowd. Come to the festival at least.
Straighten that stall. The fish man will measure it, I promise you.
The lanterns are going up! Step back, look. Isn't that something?
The whole street's ready, and an hour early. This might be the best festival yet.
Look down the street. Every lantern straight. I could cry. I will later.
Half the stalls up and no lanterns. We'll open in the dark and call it atmosphere.
Not finished. The committee will grumble. They grumble every year anyway.
Festival setup, done. If the lanterns stay up tonight, that's on you. In a good way.
{client} says the street looks wonderful. Logged. Enjoy the festival.
These strings don't go post to post. They go roof to roof, three storeys up. Mind your footing.
A whole crate of lanterns is missing from {store}. It was on the inventory this morning.
The fireworks crate needs to cross the street. The crowded street. Gently. Very, very gently.
Light the Street Lamps at Dusk
The lamplighter, {client}, is short a pair of hands tonight. Light the district's lamps from {lamps} on, before full dark. {pay}.
Oil, wick, flame, glass, in that order. Start at {lamps} and work down the hill. Don't skip one.
Dusk to dark is quicker than you think. Once the first star's out, you're late.
Good. Here's the oil can and the taper. Don't light your sleeve.
Thank you. The old lady at the corner waits up for her lamp. Do hers first.
Then half the street goes dark tonight. I'll do what I can.
No? I'll do it alone and finish at midnight. As usual.
That's the hill done. Keep going down the lane.
Trim the wick shorter. A tall flame smokes the glass black.
Every lamp burning before dark. The street looks like a string of pearls.
Look at that. People are walking slower. That's what light does.
Half the street's dark. Folk will stub their toes and blame me. Never mind.
Too late for some of them. We'll light the rest and call it done.
Lamps lit, the whole district. You smell of lamp oil. Logged.
{client} says not one lamp missed. That's a lamplighter's highest praise.
The can's dry and half the street's still dark. More oil, from the market, before it's black out here.
Someone down the lane is trying doors in the dark. Quietly, one after another.
Gate Logbook, Main Gate
The gate guards at {gate} want help logging the day's travellers. Neat writing preferred. {pay}.
Name, village, reason, how long. Every traveller, every cart. Check the pass, then write it down.
Ink stays in the book, not on the pass. Some of these papers came a long way.
Good. Here's the logbook. Write small, we've a long day.
Right. Stand where I can see you. If anything's odd, you call me.
Back to writing with one hand and checking with the other. Wonderful.
No matter. The gate opens every day. You'll get another chance.
That's thirty logged. Your hand cramped yet?
Neat writing. My chief will think I've finally learned to spell.
A full day logged, not a single blot. The chief will frame this page.
Every traveller in the book. Good eyes, good hand. Come back any time.
Gaps in the log. The chief will have questions. I'll answer them.
A messy page. The gate's a busy place. You'll get the hang of it.
Gate logbook, done. The gate guards say you've got a steady hand. Logged, and paid.
Signed off. {client} says your page was the neatest all week.
That cart's papers say "dried fish, light load". So why is it sitting so low on its wheels?
This traveller booked an inn and has no idea where it is. Or what it's called, exactly.
Papers in order, cart too heavy. Wave it through, or hold it for the guards to search?
Bring the Harvest In Before the Rain
{client} needs the harvest at {field} in the barn before the rain. Rain's due tomorrow. {pay}.
Every sheaf from {field} into {barn} before the rain comes. Wet grain rots. Rotten grain is a hungry winter.
Cut low, tie tight, stack it on the cart in rows. The ox knows the way to the barn.
Good. Sickles are sharp, so watch your fingers.
Thank you. Rice balls at noon and a full bowl at dusk. That's the deal.
Then we'll cut till dark and hope the clouds hold off.
No? The whole family's out in the field already. We'll manage.
Smell that? Rain on the wind. Faster now.
Another cartload. That's more than we did all yesterday.
All in, all dry. Let it pour now. Thank you, all of you.
Every sheaf under cover. We eat this winter because of today.
The rain beat us. Some of it's lost. The rest we'll dry by the fire.
Not all of it. But enough, maybe. We'll see.
Harvest's in. {client} sent a sack of rice with the report. Shall I share it out?
Done before the rain. That's a farmer who'll eat well and remember the Leaf kindly. Logged.
Deer from the clan forest got to the field first. Shoo them gently. They're the Nara's, not ours.
Thunder over the hills. The rain's coming early. Half the field to cut in half the time.
A crack like a branch snapping. The cart's axle is broken, and it's fully loaded.
Clear the Bandit Camp
C-rank. A bandit camp at {camp} has been robbing the outer farms. {client} brought the complaint. Clear it out. {pay}.
They come down from {camp} every few nights. Took my seed rice, my neighbour's ox, half the village's tools.
There's a lookout at {lookout}. Get past that and the rest are in the hollow.
Thank you. I'll tell the other farms help is coming. They'll sleep tonight.
Good. Be careful. They're rough, and there are more of them than you'd think.
Then we keep sitting up with pitchforks every night. Until something happens.
No? We'll bar the doors and hope. It hasn't worked yet.
Did you see the lookout? Are they still up there?
Smoke from the hollow. They're cooking. That means they're all in.
The camp's empty and our tools are back. You've given the farms their nights back.
Is that my ox? It is! You found my ox! Thank you, all of you.
They're still up there. We'll keep the lamps lit and the dogs loose.
It didn't work. They'll be angrier now. I'm not blaming you. I'm just afraid.
Bandit camp cleared. The farms outside the wall have sent a thank-you in the form of a very large radish. Logged.
C-rank done, everyone back on their own feet. That's the result I like best. Paid.
There are people tied up by the fire. Farmhands. Get them clear before the fighting reaches them.
The leader's running! Straight for the hills, leaving the rest behind. After them!
These aren't bandits. Look at their hands, their boots. Farmers, from a village that burned. Starving.
They're thin as rakes and fighting with hoes. Whatever they've done, these are farmers, not raiders.
Starving farmers, not hardened thieves. Talk them down and show mercy, or arrest them all?
Bear on the Outer Training Grounds
C-rank. A bear has moved into {ground} and won't leave. {client} wants it gone before the squads come back. {pay}.
Big, brown, and sitting in the middle of {ground} like it pays rent. Nobody can train with that out there.
Move it on, back to the hills. Hurt it only if you must. It's just a bear doing bear things.
Good. Don't run if it charges. Or do. I'm not a bear expert.
Thank you. I'll keep everyone off the grounds till you're back.
Then the squads train in the village yards for another week. Crowded and grumpy.
No? Fine. The bear doesn't mind waiting. It's very patient.
Is it still by the target posts? It likes the target posts.
Claw marks on the fence. Fresh ones. It's close.
Gone, back to the hills, and nobody hurt. Including the bear. Good.
The grounds are clear. The squads can come back tomorrow. Thank you.
Still there. Still eating the straw dummies. We'll try again.
It won't budge. Come back when you've rested.
Bear moved on from the outer grounds. The training squads are delighted. The bear, less so. Logged.
C-rank, done. No one mauled. I like a report with no hospital forms attached.
{client}'s beehives at {honey}. A bear will follow honey anywhere. Even away from here.
Cubs in the bushes. Two of them. And their mother knows exactly how close you are.
Giant Boar in the Fields
C-rank. A giant boar is wrecking the farms at {fields}. Track it to its wallow and stop it. {client} is desperate. {pay}.
It's the size of an ox. Tore up three fields and a fence. My children won't go outside.
The tracks lead towards {lair}. Mud, mostly. And broken saplings.
Thank you. Its tusks are as long as my arm. Please, be careful.
Good. Bring it down or drive it off. Either way, I can plant again.
Then we lose the spring crop. We've lost worse. Not much worse.
No? I'll build the fence higher. It'll break it again.
That's its track. See how deep? Heavier than a horse.
The smell from the wallow. You can't miss it.
The fields are safe. The children can play outside again. Thank you.
It's done. I can plant tomorrow. I didn't think I'd be able to say that.
It's still out there, and angry now. We'll keep the children in.
Not today. We'll mend what we can and wait.
Boar dealt with. The farmer sent a basket of turnips. I'm told that's the highest honour. Logged.
C-rank, done. That's a field that will feed people this summer. Good work.
Piglets. A whole litter, tucked behind her. She's a mother, and she's been driven out of her own forest.
A second set of tracks crosses the first. Bigger. There are two of them.
A mother with piglets, driven from her forest. Drive her off somewhere safe, or fight to end the threat?
Wolves at the Outer Farms
C-rank. Wolves are taking livestock from the outer farms at night. Guard {pen}, then find the den. {pay}.
Three goats and a calf this week. They come after midnight, quiet as smoke. My dogs are terrified.
Watch {pen} tonight. When they come, follow them home. The den's somewhere above {den}.
Thank you. I'll leave a lamp in the window. Don't let it fool you, I'll be hiding under the bed.
Good. Take my lantern. And this stick. It's a good stick.
Then we lose another goat tonight. And tomorrow.
No? We'll bring the animals into the house. It's crowded, but it's safe.
Did you hear them? Out past the stream. Howling.
Tracks in the frost. Five, maybe six of them.
Not a single animal taken last night. First time in weeks. Thank you.
The wolves are gone from the hills above us. I don't know how you did it. Thank you.
Another pen broken. We'll keep watch ourselves. It's all we can do.
They're still out there. Come back when you're ready. Please.
Wolf trouble at the outer farms, settled. You look like you've been up all night. Because you have. Logged.
C-rank, done. The farmers say the hills are quiet again. Paid.
Smoke on the hills above the den. Campfires. A bandit gang's fires drove the wolves down to the farms.
That wolf at the front. It's the size of a pony. The rest of the pack follow it like a shadow.
Bodyguard for a Noble Child
C-rank. A visiting noble, {client}, wants a squad to guard their child for a day in the village, from {inn} to {market}. {pay}.
My child wants to see the village. The market, the shops, the Hokage Rock. Keep them safe and keep them happy.
We stay at {inn}. Collect the child there at nine. Return by sunset, and not a moment later.
Very good. My child is curious, and has no sense of danger. That is your job.
Excellent. Do try to make it fun. The last guards were dreadfully dull.
How disappointing. We will tour the village with our own guards, I suppose.
I see. The Leaf is busier than I was told.
Is my child enjoying the day? Good. And safe? Better.
They wrote to me already. "Bought a wooden kunai." I did not approve that.
Home safe and full of stories. My child says the Leaf is the best place in the world. Thank you.
A happy day and not a hair out of place. You have my gratitude, and my good word with your Hokage.
My child is safe, but it was too close. I expected better from the Leaf.
We will be leaving early. I'm sure you understand.
Noble child, returned in one piece. {client} sent a very formal letter. Mostly polite. Logged.
Bodyguard C-rank, done. A happy child and a calm parent. Diplomacy on legs. Good work.
The child was right here a second ago. Gone. Slipped off to see the village alone.
Those men by the stall have been following since the inn. Someone's paid them to take the child.
Race for the Cat Burglar
C-rank, contested. A cat burglar's working {rooftops}. I've sent two squads. First to bring them in gets the pay: {pay}.
Six houses this month, always the rooftops, always gone before the dogs bark. The other squad left ten minutes ago.
The burglar's hideout is somewhere around {hideout}. Nobody's found it. Yet.
Good. Run. The other squad is already out the door.
Right. Bring them in alive, unbruised if possible, and before the others do.
Then the other squad takes it uncontested. Easy money for them.
No? I'll tell them they've got the whole field. They'll be smug.
Sighted on the bakery roof ten minutes ago. Heading east.
The other squad came past here at a sprint. They're ahead of you.
Caught, and before the other squad! The rooftops are safe again.
You beat them to it. They'll be sulking for a week.
The burglar's slipped away, and the other squad's still looking. Not today.
The other squad got there first. Shake hands. It's still the Leaf.
Cat burglar, in custody. And you beat the other squad. I'm not supposed to have favourites. I do. Logged.
Contest closed. The rooftops are quiet. Pay's yours.
That tip about the east alley was {rival_squad}'s doing. Wrong street. Deliberately.
The burglar's too quick for either squad alone. {rival_squad} are nodding. Work together, split the credit.
Sealed Message to the Border Post
C-rank. Rush a sealed message to {post} within the day. Through {pass}, no stops. {pay}.
Sealed, and stays sealed. Hand it to the post commander at {post}. Nobody else.
Take the pass at {pass}. It's the fastest way, which is also why it's the one people watch.
Good. Here's the case. It doesn't leave your body until you're at the post.
Right. Run light, eat on the move. Sleep when you're back.
Then I send it with the next squad and hope it's not too late.
No? It'll have to wait. The border hates waiting.
At the pass already? Good time. Keep moving.
The seal's still whole? Good. Don't stop to look at it every mile.
Delivered, sealed, inside the day. The post commander sends thanks.
Clean run. Exactly how a courier mission should go.
Too late for it to matter. We'll find another way.
The message didn't get through. Come back and we'll talk about what happened.
Courier run, done. The border post says the seal was intact and the runners looked exhausted. Both good signs. Logged.
Message delivered on time. Go and sleep. You've earned that before the pay.
Two figures at the pass, waiting, watching the road. Scouts, and they know exactly what you're carrying.
The commander wants you to wait. There's an answer to carry back, and it's being written now.
Medicine for the Border Village
C-rank, two days. Medicine and supplies for the healer at {healer}, by the hill road at {road}. {pay}.
Fever remedies, bandages, a crate of salves. The border village's healer is nearly out of everything.
The crates are fragile and the road at {road} is rough. Slow on the hills, quick on the flat.
Thank you. There are people waiting on this. Real people. Children.
Good. The cart's loaded. The horse is called Biscuit. Don't ask me why.
Then I'll send it with a trader and pray it arrives.
No? I'll wait for another squad. The healer can't wait long.
Crates all still roped? Check the knots at every stop.
Halfway. The healer will have sent someone to watch the road for you.
Every crate delivered. The healer wrote to say three fevers broke the first night.
It got there. All of it. You've no idea how many people that helps.
Not everything arrived. The healer will make do. They always do, out there.
It didn't get through. We'll send another cart. Thank you for trying.
Medical delivery to the border, done. The healer sent a letter. It's mostly gratitude and a list of what to send next. Logged.
C-rank, done. That's medicine where it was needed. The best kind of mission.
The cart's lighter. You turned your back to water the horse and two crates are gone.
Thugs on the only bridge, with a sign and a box. A "toll", they say. For crossing their bridge.
The sky's gone black over the pass. Storm. Get the cart under the overhang and wait it out.
Pay the thugs' toll and keep the medicine moving, or fight your way across the bridge?
Kiln Pottery to the Border Market
C-rank, two days. The kiln family's best pottery from {kiln} to the market at {market}, unbroken. {pay}.
This is a year's best work. Packed in straw, roped in crates. Not one chip, please, or it's worthless.
The road at {road} has a reputation. Thieves know what good pottery fetches at the border.
Thank you. Drive the cart like it's carrying eggs. Because it might as well be.
Good. If anyone asks what's in the crates, say turnips.
Then we miss the market. A year's work sits in the shed.
No? I'll wait for the next squad. The market won't wait long.
Still ringing true when you tap the crates? Good.
Halfway to {market}. Slow on the downhill.
Every piece arrived whole. They sold out by noon on the first day. Thank you.
Not a crack. My grandmother would have hugged you. I might.
Broken. Half of it. A year's work in shards on the road.
It didn't reach the market. We'll start again. Potters always start again.
Pottery delivered whole. That's harder than any fight, if you ask me. Logged.
C-rank, done. {client} says the market bought every piece. Good work.
Rope across the road and figures in the trees. Thieves, and they know what's under that straw.
A rival workshop's master is shouting across the market: the glaze on these pots was stolen from them.
Supplies to the Hill Outpost
C-rank, two days. A cart of supplies to the watch outpost at {outpost}, up the trail at {trail}. {pay}.
Rice, oil, bandages and arrows. The outpost has been on short rations for a week.
The trail at {trail} is steep and narrow. Mind the cart wheels on the switchbacks.
Good. The watch up there will be glad to see you. They don't get many visitors.
Right. Load is checked. Go.
Then the outpost tightens its belt another notch. They're used to it.
No? I'll find a squad that will. Soon, I hope.
Switchbacks ahead. Push from the back, pull from the front.
The outpost will have seen your dust by now.
Supplies delivered. The watch sends thanks and a request for more pickles next time.
The outpost is stocked for a month. Good work.
The supplies didn't reach the top. The outpost will be hungry.
Not today. We'll send another cart. Rest first.
Outpost supplied. The Chunin up there wrote "thank you" in very large letters. Logged.
C-rank, done. A fed outpost is a watchful outpost. Paid.
Half the outpost is flat on their mats with fever. The ones still standing are swaying.
The cart road's gone. A landslide took it overnight. The crates go up the rest of the way by hand.
The Signboard Taker
C-rank. A wandering swordsman is beating the village's dojos one by one and taking their signboards. {client} wants it stopped. {pay}.
Four dojos beaten. Four signboards taken. A challenge notice was nailed to {dojo} this morning.
The Gekko don't hire help for swords. But this one is good, and we're tired of losing boards.
Good. Watch the footwork, not the blade. The blade lies. The feet don't.
Thank you. Bring the signboards home. They mean more than they look.
Then the swordsman takes another board tonight.
Understood. We'll face it ourselves. We'll lose, but we'll face it.
The challenge notice says sunset. Be there early.
Not every swordsman is what they seem. Watch the sleeves.
The signboards are back on their walls. Every dojo in the Leaf owes you.
Well fought. The Gekko will remember this.
Another board gone. We'll train harder. That's all we can do.
Not today. The swordsman is still out there. So are we.
Dojo challenge, settled. The signboards are home. {client} bowed to me. I didn't know what to do. Logged.
C-rank, done. The dojos are calling it a fine duel. Pay's here.
The swordsman kneels and lays the blade down. All this was only for a worthy opponent. And now, a request: to be taught.
A glint at the swordsman's sleeve. Needles, and the tips are wet. Poison.
Beaten, the swordsman waits. Take the signboards and send them off, or agree to teach them?
Escort a Trader, East Road
C-rank, two days. Escort {client} and a cart of goods along the east road to {waystation}. Bandits reported near {bend}. {pay}.
Silk, salt and lacquer boxes, all the way to {waystation}. Two days on the east road. I've heard stories about that road.
We'll camp at {camp} the first night. Then the bridge, then the waystation. Easy, if nothing happens.
Good. I walk slowly and talk a lot. You'll get used to both.
Excellent. I'll pay for the first night's meal at the waystation. A good one.
Then I'll go alone. Or not go. Probably not go.
No? I'll ask another squad. Or hire some muscle in the market. Cheaper, louder.
Is that the bend? I always hold my breath at the bend.
The cart's holding up. The axle grumbles, but it always grumbles.
The waystation! And every box intact. You're the best escort I've ever paid for.
We made it. I'll tell every trader on this road to ask for your squad.
We lost half the cart. I'm alive, though. That counts for something.
It didn't go well. I'll turn back. Thank you for keeping me breathing.
Escort to the east waystation, done. {client} sent a bolt of silk for the desk. It's very nice. Logged.
C-rank complete. Trader safe, goods safe, squad home. That's the whole job.
The bridge is gone. Washed out. The ford's the only way now, and it's slow and open on both sides.
Movement past the firelight. They've come back, at night, for the cart.
A traveller on the road, alone, begging to walk with the cart. For safety, they say.
One bandit didn't run. Tied up by the cart, they swear they'll never come back. Hand them over at the waystation, or let them go?
Escort a Scholar to the Border
C-rank, two days. Escort {client}, a scholar, through the hills to {village}. The road goes over {pass}. {pay}.
I have business in the border village. Books to see, people to ask. I've never walked the hills before.
Two days, they tell me. Over {pass}, a night at {camp}, then down to {village}. How hard can it be?
Splendid. I've packed three books and one spare sock. Is that enough?
Thank you. I promise to complain only about the important things.
Then I'll wait for the next squad. My research has waited this long.
No? I'll read about the hills instead. Much less walking.
Is it always this steep? Don't answer that.
I've filled four pages with notes already. The wildflowers here are extraordinary.
We're here. I can't feel my feet, but we're here. Thank you, truly.
Safe in the border village, and with my books dry. You're a credit to the Leaf.
I'll go home. The hills won this time. Thank you for getting me back.
It didn't work out. I'm not cut out for mountains, it seems.
Scholar delivered safely. {client} wrote a whole page about how brave you were. It's quite flowery. Logged.
C-rank, done. A client who arrived healthier than they left. That's good escort work.
{client} is pale and sweating at the pass, sitting down every ten steps. The hills have got to them.
By the fire, {client} goes quiet, then admits the real reason for the trip. Harmless, and private. "Please don't tell anyone."
{client} asked you to keep the secret. Keep it, or put it in the mission report?
Guard a Caravan, East Road
C-rank, two days. Guard {client}'s three-cart caravan on the east road as far as {waystation}. Raiders are active. {pay}.
Three carts, two drivers I trust, and a lot of road. We camp at {camp} and reach {waystation} the second evening.
The raiders on this road hit fast and run. Keep your eyes on the treeline and your hands near your kunai.
Good. You'll ride the middle cart. Best view, worst seat.
Thank you. My drivers are {hand_a} and {hand_b}. They know the road. Listen to them.
Then I'll wait. The goods will wait too, more or less.
No? I'll double the drivers and hope for the best.
First day done. We're on schedule. Don't jinx it.
The oxen are nervous. They smell something we don't.
Three carts in, three carts whole. I'll hire your squad again, for every trip.
Every crate accounted for at the waystation. That's a good guard.
We lost a cart. Maybe more. At least we're alive.
It went badly. I'll be counting losses for a week.
Caravan guarded to the waystation. {client} is ordering their next run through us. Logged.
C-rank, done. Two days, three carts, one tired squad. Paid.
A mirror flash from the second cart. Someone in the caravan is signalling the raiders.
This wheel's been cut halfway through. Clean cut, fresh sawdust. Somebody did it in the night.
The signals came from inside the caravan. Accuse {hand_a}, accuse {hand_b}, or say nothing until you're sure?
Festival Watch: Pickpockets
C-rank. A pickpocket gang is working the festival crowd on {street}. {client} wants it stopped tonight. {pay}.
Four purses gone last night and three the night before. They work in pairs. One bumps, one lifts.
Walk the crowd on {street}. Watch the hands, not the faces. Faces always look innocent.
Good. Wear something festive. A squad in uniform scares the thieves off before you can catch them.
Thank you. If you can, enjoy a little of the festival too. Just a little.
Then I'll warn people to hold their purses tight and hope.
No? The gang will have a very good night, then.
Anything? I saw a pair near the goldfish stall acting oddly.
Another purse gone by the lantern arch. They're bold.
The gang's caught and the purses are back with their owners. The festival can breathe.
A quiet night! Not one purse lost after you caught them. Thank you.
They got away with half the market's takings. We'll do better next year.
Not tonight. They're slippery. Thank you for trying.
Pickpocket gang, caught. Did you at least eat some yakitori while you were out there? Logged.
C-rank, done. The festival committee is very relieved. Paid.
The purses were a distraction. The gang's real target is the fireworks crate behind the stage.
{guest}'s child has slipped the guards to see the stalls alone. Somewhere in this crowd.
Smugglers at the Ford
C-rank, night work. A smuggling crew crosses the river at {ford} after dark. Hide in {hide}, wait, and stop them. {pay}.
Untaxed metal, mostly. Bad blades that undercut honest smiths. They cross {ford} at moonrise.
The reeds at {hide} are good cover. Cold and wet, but good cover.
Good. Dark clothes, no lamps. And don't sneeze.
Thank you. The Hagane forges can't compete with stolen metal. Stop them.
Then they cross again tonight, and the night after.
No? I'll report it to the guard again. They'll do nothing again.
Moonrise soon. Stay low in the reeds.
Hear that? Oars. Quiet ones. They're coming.
The crew's caught and the cargo seized. The honest forges thank you.
That ford will be quiet for a long while now. Good.
They crossed. We'll see their blades in the market by next week.
Not tonight. They were quicker than we thought.
Smuggling crew, stopped. You're wet to the waist. Reeds, was it? Logged.
C-rank, done. {client} says the forge district will sleep easier. Paid.
Not metal. The crates are full of animals. Rare ones, crammed into cages far too small.
The first boat's empty. A decoy. The real one is crossing downstream right now!
Cramped cages full of rare animals. Free them here by the river, or hand them over as evidence?
The Haunted Waystation Inn
C-rank, two days. The inn at {inn} has a ghost story, and travellers who never checked out. {client} wants it looked into. {pay}.
Footsteps at night, cold drafts, a face at the window. Guests leave in the dark without paying. Some don't leave at all.
Stay a night at {inn}. See it for yourselves. And please, please tell me it's not real.
Thank you. Your rooms are free, of course. Room six is the worst one. You're in room six.
Good. Don't go in the cellar alone. Don't go in the cellar at all, actually.
Then I'll lose more guests. And maybe my mind.
No? I'll ask the priest to come again. It didn't work last time.
Did you hear it last night? The knocking? Tell me you heard it.
Cold spot on the stairs again. I don't go up there after dark.
No ghost. Just people, and they're gone now. My inn is mine again.
I can sleep through the night! I've forgotten what that feels like. Thank you.
The knocking's still there. Maybe it is a ghost. Maybe I'll sell.
Nothing solved. I'll keep the lamps lit all night again.
Haunted inn, investigated. No ghosts on file. I'm relieved. I don't know what form I'd use. Logged.
C-rank, done. The waystation inn is open for business, minus the haunting. Paid.
Fresh footprints in the cellar dust, and a passage behind the casks. A gang has been robbing the sleeping guests.
{client} finally admits it: grandfather made the ghost up, years ago, to bring curious guests in. It worked too well.
Stakeout: Warehouse Thefts
C-rank. Goods keep vanishing from {warehouse}. Interview the staff, stake it out, find out who. {pay}.
A crate a week, never more. No broken locks. Whoever it is has a key, or knows where one hangs.
Three people work nights: {night_guard}, {clerk} and {porter}. I trust them all. That's the problem.
Thank you. Be fair to them. Whoever it isn't deserves that.
Good. Watch the back door. That's where I'd go.
Then I'll change the locks and hope. Again.
No? I'll keep counting crates and losing sleep.
Have you spoken to all three yet? What did they say?
Another crate missing last night. Right under our noses.
Now I know. It hurts, but I know. Thank you.
The thefts have stopped. The warehouse feels like mine again.
Still vanishing. I'll be suspecting everyone forever now.
No answer. I'll have to look at all of them differently. I hate that.
Warehouse thefts, solved. {client} is relieved and a little sad. That's how these usually end. Logged.
C-rank, done. Stakeouts are mostly waiting. You waited well. Paid.
The key that opens the back door hangs on {night_guard}'s belt. And the mud on those sandals matches the alley.
The ledger's been changed in {clerk}'s hand. Every missing crate, written out of the books afterwards.
{porter} carries crates out every night, and one more always goes out the back than came in the front.
You've heard all three and seen the clues. Name the thief: {night_guard}, {clerk} or {porter}?
Keep the Peace at the Stream
C-rank. Two hamlets near the border are fighting over {stream}. Keep the peace until the magistrate comes. {client} asked for us. {pay}.
They've dammed {stream} above our fields. My rice is drying out. {other_headman} says it was always theirs.
Hear us both, if you must. Just make sure nobody gets hurt before the magistrate arrives.
Thank you. You'll see we're in the right. Look at our fields.
Good. My people are angry. Your being here will calm them.
Then someone will get hurt. I can feel it coming.
No? The magistrate is a week away. It's a long week.
Did you talk to {other_headman}? What did they say? Lies, I expect.
The weir is still blocked. My people are gathering with spades.
Water flows to both hamlets. Nobody hurt. The magistrate will have little to do.
Peace. Fragile, but peace. Thank you for listening to both of us.
It came to blows. The magistrate will have a lot to say.
Nothing settled. Both sides angrier than before.
Water dispute, calmed. The magistrate arrived to find almost nothing to do. That's a compliment. Logged.
C-rank, done. Diplomacy is harder than fighting. You managed it. Paid.
Strangers with clubs on the weir. One headman has hired muscle to settle the stream by force.
Look at the banks. Cracked mud a hand's width down. It's a dry season, and there's barely enough for one hamlet.
The magistrate isn't here yet, and someone must decide. Share the water, give it upstream, or give it downstream?
Border Patrol with a Chunin
C-rank. Walk a stretch of the border with {client}, checking the markers at {markers} and the watch at {post}. {pay}.
We walk the line from {markers} to {post}. Every stone checked, every post visited. It's long and mostly dull.
Mostly. If you see someone on the wrong side of a marker, you tell me before you do anything.
Good. Bring water and good sandals. We'll walk a long way.
Right. Quiet on the line. Voices carry along the ridge.
Fine. I'll walk it alone. It's quieter that way.
No? Another squad will come. The border isn't going anywhere.
That's the fourth marker. Straight and unmoved. Good.
The watch post is past the next ridge. Keep pace.
Line walked, markers checked, posts visited. A clean patrol.
Good work. You kept your eyes open. That's all a patrol really is.
We'll turn back. The patrol's compromised. Report it as it happened.
Not a clean walk. We'll report it and send another squad.
Border patrol, done. {client} says your squad kept up and kept quiet. Logged.
C-rank complete. The line is where it should be. Paid.
Two figures by the watch post with a drawing board. Foreign scouts, mapping every post on the line.
{lost} is crouched beyond the marker stones, a Genin from another village, lost and very frightened.
Guard a Shop Through the Sale
C-rank. {client} at {shop} is being threatened by a rival's hired thugs. Protect the shop through the week's big sale. {pay}.
They broke a window last week and told my customers to shop elsewhere. My stall, at {shop}. My living.
I know who's paying them. {rival}. Nobody will say so out loud.
Thank you. Stand where people can see you. That alone might be enough.
Good. If they come, they come at closing. That's when they always come.
Then I'll close for the week. And lose the sale, and maybe the shop.
No? I'll board the windows and pray.
They walked past twice this morning. Looking. Just looking.
Sales are good! People feel safe with a squad here.
The sale's over and the shop's whole. Best week I've had all year.
No broken windows, no frightened customers. Thank you.
They got in. Broken stock, frightened customers. I don't know what I'll do.
It didn't work. Maybe nothing would have. Thank you for standing with me.
Shop protected through the sale. The market's talking about it. Logged.
C-rank, done. Sometimes guarding is about standing still and being seen. Paid.
The rival's man leans close. Twice the fee to be somewhere else at closing. Coins already in hand.
The ledger tells a different story. {client} started this feud, years ago, by undercutting {rival}.
Twice the fee to look away. Refuse the coins, or take them?
Both shopkeepers share the blame. Bring them together to talk it out, or stand by your client?
Recover a Stolen Heirloom
C-rank. {client}'s family heirloom was stolen and turned up at a pawnshop in the border village, at {pawn}. Recover it. {pay}.
A lacquered box, black with a gold crane on the lid. My family has kept it for five generations.
Someone saw it in the back of {pawn}. They won't sell it back. They say they never had it.
Thank you. It's not worth much to anyone else. It's worth everything to us.
Good. The pawnbroker isn't alone. There's a whole ring behind that counter. Be careful.
Then it's gone. Five generations, and I'm the one who lost it.
No? I'll keep writing to the magistrate. For all the good it does.
Did you see it? Is it there? Is it whole?
The ledger says they bought it a month ago. From whom, I wonder.
That's it. That's the crane. Thank you. You've no idea.
Home. Back on the shelf where it belongs. My grandmother would weep.
It's still in their hands. Or sold on. I'll never know.
Gone. Thank you for trying. It mattered that someone tried.
Heirloom recovered. {client} came by to say thank you in person. Twice. Logged.
C-rank, done. Some things matter far more than their price. Paid.
This box in the back room is a copy. Wrong weight, wrong lacquer. The real one is out on the counter, in plain sight.
Boots on the stairs. The pawnbroker's men are back early, and the back room has one door.
Find the Missing Woodcutter
C-rank, rescue. A woodcutter didn't come home from {woods} last night. {client}'s household is frantic. Find them. {pay}.
Our woodcutter went up the path at {woods} yesterday morning and never came back. The axe is gone too.
Follow the path. There'll be fresh chips where the cutting stopped. Please hurry.
Thank you. Take this blanket. And this water. And please, please hurry.
Good. I'll keep the fire high so you can see the house from the hill.
Then I'll go up myself. In the dark, if I have to.
No? We'll gather the neighbours with torches.
Any sign? Chips, footprints? Anything?
The light's going. Please keep looking.
Home! Hurt, but home. Thank you. I'll never forget this.
You found them. Alive. I don't know how to thank you.
Nothing. We'll keep searching at first light.
You came back without them. I know you tried. I know.
Missing woodcutter, found and home. The hospital says a broken leg and a lot of luck. Logged.
C-rank rescue, done. The best reports are the ones where everyone comes home. Paid.
A shout from below. The woodcutter fell into the ravine at {ravine}, and the only way down is the cliff face.
Howling, closer than it should be. The wolves smelled the blood before you found the woodcutter.
Track the Thief into the Forest
C-rank. A thief robbed {client}'s stall at {shop} and fled into the forest along {forest}. Track them down. {pay}.
Grabbed the cash box and a sack of rice, then ran for the trees at {forest}. Fast, and small.
The tracks start at my back door. After that, the forest. I don't know the forest.
Thank you. The box has my mark on the lid. A circle with a line.
Good. Bring my money back. And the rice, if it's still whole.
Then it's gone. A month's takings, gone.
No? I'll put a lock on the door. Too late, as always.
Found the trail? Good. It was going towards the stream when I lost it.
The forest's thick out there. Don't get lost yourselves.
My box! And most of the coins. Thank you. I didn't think I'd see it again.
Found, and brought back. You're better at this than the guards.
The trail went cold. So did my hopes. Thank you anyway.
Gone into the forest for good, then. I'll start saving again.
Thief tracked and stall money returned. You've pine needles in your collar. Logged.
C-rank, done. Tracking's patience more than speed. You had both. Paid.
The tracks stop dead at the stream. The thief doubled back through the water to throw off the dogs.
The thief is a child. Thin, frightened, guarding the rice like treasure. It was for a sick parent at home.
A runaway child stealing for a sick parent. Bring them in as the job says, or plead their case to {client}?
Persimmon Picking, Tall Trees
{client}'s persimmons at {orchard} are ripe at the very tops. Tree walking welcome, ladders provided. {pay}.
The low fruit's picked. The best ones are up top in {orchard}, where my ladder won't reach.
Twist, don't pull, and lay them in the basket stem up. A bruised persimmon is a sad persimmon.
Wonderful. Mind the thin branches. Persimmon wood snaps without warning.
Good. You'll take a basket home after. Hang them to dry and they'll be sweet by winter.
Then the birds get the top ones again. They always do.
No? I'll ask my nephew. He climbs like a monkey and complains like one too.
Look at the colour on that one! Careful, careful. Into the basket.
Your feet are stuck to the trunk like it's the ground. Show-off.
Baskets full to the brim and not one bruise. You've a light touch.
The best crop in years, and it all came down in one piece. Take some home.
Half the fruit on the grass. Well, the crows will be happy.
Not many baskets today. Never mind. The tree will try again next autumn.
Orchard job, done. There's a persimmon on my desk now. I'm choosing to think it's for me.
{client} says the top branches are bare for the first time in years. Logged.
A wasp nest hangs in the best tree, right where the ripest fruit is. Of course it does.
A child climbed up after you and now won't move. Clinging to a branch, very high, very quiet.
Medicinal Herbs, Outer Slopes
The hospital needs medicinal herbs from {slope}. {client} of the Suzuran will show you which. Deliver to {hospital}. {pay}.
