Feverfew, mugwort, the little blue-flowered one. Here's a drawing. Cut above the root so it grows back.
Bring them to {hospital} before evening. Wilted herbs lose half their good.
Good. Here's a knife and a cloth bag. Not a sack. They bruise in a sack.
Thank you. My family has gathered on that slope for six generations. Treat it kindly.
Understood. I'll go myself at dawn. The herbs are best then anyway.
No? The medics will make do with dried stock for another week.
That's the right leaf. See the fine hairs underneath? Good eye.
Leave a few plants in every patch. Always leave some for next year.
A full bag, every one the right plant. The hospital will be very glad.
Clean cuts, fresh leaves. You'd make a fine herbalist, if you ever tire of kunai.
Too few, and some of these are wilted. We'll go again tomorrow.
Not enough for the hospital's order. It happens. The slope will keep.
Herbs delivered to the hospital. You smell of mint and mud. Logged.
{client} checked every stem and found nothing wrong. That's the Suzuran stamp of approval.
Wait. These two leaves look the same, but one smells bitter. A poisonous lookalike. Check every stem.
The best patch on the slope has a snake coiled right in the middle of it, sunning itself.
Orderly, One Day on the Wards
The hospital wants orderlies for a day on {ward}. Linens, meals, errands for the medics. {client} will meet you. {pay}.
Fresh sheets on every bed in {ward}, meals at noon and six, and run where the medics send you.
Speak softly, walk softly. Some of these patients haven't slept in days.
Thank you. Wash your hands at the basin. Every time you enter a room.
Good. If anyone asks you a medical question, fetch a medic. Don't guess.
We'll stretch the shift, then. We always do.
Understood. The wards will manage, somehow.
The sheets in room four are done? Good. Room five needs water.
The patient by the window says you're very polite. Keep it up.
Every bed clean, every meal served. The medics got their breaks for once.
You were a real help today. The patients noticed. So did I.
A hard shift, and some things fell through. Go home. Rest. Hospitals are like that.
Not the smoothest day. Nobody was hurt by it, though. That's what matters here.
Orderly shift, done. The medics asked if you could come back. Twice.
Hospital job, logged. Don't worry, that smell of disinfectant fades in a day.
Bed twelve is empty. {wanderer} has wandered out in slippers and a gown, and could be anywhere.
The medics are out of a herb only the Suzuran gardens grow. Run to {garden} for more.
Riverside Laundry for the Inn
The washers at {bank} have the inn's laundry and too few hands. Wash, wring, dry, deliver to {inn}. {pay}.
Sheets from {inn}, a mountain of them. Scrub on the stones, rinse downstream, wring till your arms ache.
Whites first, coloured last, never together. The inn counts every sheet back.
Good! Roll your trousers up, the water's cold this time of year.
Here's a washboard. You'll be singing the washing songs by noon. Everyone does.
More scrubbing for us, then. Our hands are tough. They'd have to be.
No? The inn's guests will sleep on yesterday's sheets. Not our problem.
Wring it harder! Like it owes you money.
That's the third basket. Hang them high, where the wind is.
Every sheet white and dry and folded. The inn will think we've hired magic.
Lovely work. Come back any washing day. We'll teach you the second verse.
Damp sheets going back to the inn. They'll complain. They always complain.
Not our best load. The river's had worse from us.
Laundry, delivered. Your hands are wrinkled like a dried plum. Logged.
{client} says you can wring a sheet properly. That's not nothing.
A gust just took a whole sheet off the line. It's sailing over the rooftops like a kite!
Someone washed a red sash with the whites. Pink, everywhere. Find which loads can still be saved.
Moving Day Across the Village
{client}'s family is moving from {old} to {new}. Boxes, furniture, and a great deal of advice. {pay}.
Everything from {old} to {new} by dark. Boxes are labelled. Mostly labelled.
Kitchen first. If we can cook tonight, we can survive anything.
Thank you! Mind the doorframe. It's lower than it looks.
Good. The boxes marked with a circle are fragile. Or is it the cross? Ask me again.
Then it'll take us three days instead of one. Wonderful.
No? We'll call the cousins. They always break something.
The kitchen's in! Now the futons. Then the rest.
Careful round that corner! No, the other corner.
Everything moved, nothing broken. We're home. A new home. Thank you.
The tea's already brewing in the new kitchen. Sit, please. You've earned it.
Half here, half there. We'll sleep in the old house one more night.
Something's broken, and we're not finished. It's still a new start. We'll get there.
Moving day, logged. You can stop carrying things now. That's a chair, not a box. Put it down.
{client} says the move went smoother than their wedding. That's a compliment, I think.
Grandmother's tea set goes by hand. Only by hand. Not in a box, not on the cart. Walk slow.
The cat does not want to move. It's found the one spot in the house nobody ever looks.
This old chest won't budge for anyone. It'll take chakra in the arms to get it off the floor.
Sort the Season's Reports
The records room at {room} has a season of mission reports to sort. By rank, then by date. {pay}.
D-ranks on the low shelves, C-ranks above. Date order. Use the tags, not the handwriting.
No reading for fun. Well. A little. Everyone does. Just keep sorting while you do it.
Good. Dust masks are in the drawer. You'll want one by the third shelf.
Excellent. I've been dreading this for a month. Here's the ledger.
Then the pile grows. It always grows.
No? I'll sort them myself in my sleep. I already dream about them.
That's spring done. Summer's the big one. Everyone takes missions in summer.
Some of these reports are written in pencil. Pencil! Put those in the box for recopying.
Every shelf in order. I could find a report from last month blindfolded. Thank you.
Perfect. I'll write your names in the log of the room. Very small. Next to the date.
Half sorted, half muddled. We'll finish another week. The shelves won't run away.
It's a muddle still. Records rooms are always a muddle. Don't take it to heart.
Records sorted. Finally. Do you know how long I've waited for that? Logged with joy.
{client} says the shelves are in order. We'll see when I next find a file in under a minute.
The ink jar tipped. Two reports are black from corner to corner. Copy them fresh before the clerk sees.
Little grey moths, all along the bottom shelf. Paper moths. They've been eating the old reports.
Storeroom Count Before Tax Day
{client} needs every item in {store} counted before the quarterly tax visit. Bring an abacus. {pay}.
Every crate in {store} counted and written in the ledger. The tax collector checks my numbers twice.
Count twice, write once. And don't move anything, I know where it all is.
Good. Here's the ledger. Neat numbers, please. Sevens with a line through them.
Thank you. Light's poor in there. Take the lamp.
I'll count it myself, then, all night. As usual.
No? Then I'll pray the collector is in a good mood.
Back shelf done? Good. The barrels are next.
That's the third time you've counted those. Something wrong?
Every number matches. The collector will have nothing to say. Lovely.
A perfect ledger. I'll sleep tonight for the first time this week.
The numbers won't come right. I'll have to explain to the collector myself.
Not finished. I'll stay up with it. Thank you anyway.
Inventory, done. You count better than half the clerks here. Don't tell them.
{client} says the ledger's spotless. Logged before tax day, even.
The numbers are short. Not by much, a little each week. Someone has been taking a few at a time.
These crates say "rice" and hold lamp oil. Half the storeroom is labelled as something else.
You know who's been taking stock from the shelves. Tell {client} who it was, or keep it to yourself?
Walk the Clinic's Ninken
The Inuzuka clinic wants its boarding ninken walked along {route} and every one brought back. Every one. {pay}.
Six dogs, six leads, one route: out along {route} and home. They know the way better than you.
Hold the leads short past the farms. They've opinions about chickens.
Good. Let them sniff your hands first. That's how you say hello.
Here are the leads. The spotted one pulls left. Always left.
More walks for me today. The dogs won't mind. My legs will.
No? Fine. They'll run the yard in circles instead.
Still six? Count them. Count them again.
They like you! The big one never leans on strangers.
Six out, six back, tired and happy. That's a good walk.
Look at them, flat out on the floor. You've worn them out. Thank you.
Not every dog came back with you. We'll find the rest. Dogs come home.
A rough walk. Leads tangled, dogs scattered. They'll forgive you.
Dog walk, done. You're covered in hair. A lot of hair. Logged.
{client} says every ninken came home. That's the whole job, and you did it.
Every nose goes up at once. The pack's caught a scent and they're bolting for the treeline!
The smallest pup won't take a step. Sits down, ears flat. It needs winning over first.
One dog's collar is gone. The one with the clan tag on it. It must have slipped off on the route.
Runaway Pet, Again
{client}'s pet has run off again. Last seen around {pet_spot}. Bring it home, preferably unscratched. {pay}.
Gone since breakfast. Not the first time. It likes {pet_spot}, I think, but it never comes when called.
Bring a dried sardine. And patience. And maybe gloves.
You'll look? Thank you. Call softly. It hides from loud voices.
Bless you. Here's the sardine. Don't eat it.
Oh. Of course. I'll go round the alleys myself at dusk.
I understand. It always turns up hungry eventually. Usually.
Anything? Paw prints? Fur on a fence?
The fishmonger says something was nosing round the bins this morning.
There you are! You bad, wonderful thing. Thank you so much.
Home, and only a little muddy. You found it. You actually found it.
No sign. I'll leave the window open tonight. Just in case.
Maybe tomorrow. Pets come home when they're ready. I'm told.
Pet returned. Don't tell me about the scratches, I can see them. Logged.
{client}'s pet is home again. Give it a month and we'll be posting this one again.
It's made a friend. Another runaway, curled up right beside it, who also needs taking home.
It didn't run off. It hid to give birth. Tiny ones, eyes shut. They'll need carrying home very gently.
{claimant} swears this pet is theirs and has been all along. Somebody's mistaken. Find out who.
Two people, one pet, and the marks don't lie. Back to {client}, or hand it to {claimant}?
Pet Sitting, One Day
{client}'s family is away for the day. Feed, brush and mind the animals at {home} at the set hours. {pay}.
Breakfast at eight, a brush at noon, supper at six. The times are pinned by the door at {home}.
Fresh water every time. And don't let it sweet-talk you into a second supper.
Thank you. Here's the key. It sticks. Lift and turn.
Good. It'll ignore you all morning, then sit on your feet by noon. Every time.
Then we'll stay home. Again.
No? I'll ask the neighbour, though they don't get on.
Has it eaten? Good. Did it sulk first? It always sulks first.
The neighbour says it's been quiet. Too quiet? No, quiet's fine.
Fed, brushed and happy. It barely noticed we were gone. Thank you.
Look how glossy! I'll ask for you every time we go away.
Missed meals and a very cross animal. Well. Nobody's hurt.
Not quite to the timetable. It'll forgive us both by morning.
Pet sitting, signed off. Fur on your sleeves and a scratch on your hand. Standard.
{client} says the animals were in better shape than when they left. Logged.
The gate's open and the bowl's untouched. It's learned to work the latch with its nose.
{neighbour} is at the fence, furious. Says this pet has been raiding their garden for weeks.
Posters in Every District
Posters for an upcoming event, one at {boards} in every district. {client} has the stack. {pay}.
One poster on every board. Straight, at eye height, four pins. Not over anyone else's.
Start at the market, finish at the gate. That way the last one's fresh for the travellers.
Good. Here are the pins. Don't lose them. They're the good pins.
Thank you. Paste pot's sticky, so mind your sleeves.
Then I'll do it myself and miss my lunch. Again.
No? The event will just have to be a surprise, then.
That's the market done? Good. Main street next.
Is that one crooked? It's crooked. Go back and fix it.
Every board, every district. Nobody can say they didn't hear about it now.
Straight as a ruler, all of them. Thank you.
Half the boards are bare. Well. Word of mouth works too.
Not every district. I'll finish the rest tomorrow.
Posters up. I passed three on my way in. Very straight. Logged.
{client} says the whole village knows now. That's what posters are for.
The poster you just pinned is gone. Torn down, and so's the last one. Someone's following you.
Look at the date. It's wrong. On every single poster in the stack.
One gust and half the stack's gone over the rooftops, fluttering in every direction.
Mend the Garden Fence
{client} needs the fence at {fence} mended. Posts from {yard}, the rest is hammer and patience. {pay}.
The fence between us and next door has been leaning for a year. Posts from {yard}, new rails, the lot.
Same line as before. Exactly the same. I don't want any trouble with the neighbours.
Good. Hammer's in the shed. Mind the roses.
Thank you. I'll bring tea when you get to the corner post. That's the hard one.
It'll lean another year, then. Until it falls on someone.
No? Fine. I'll prop it up with a broom like before.
That post's straight? Let me look. Yes. Good.
The neighbour keeps peeking over. Just smile and keep hammering.
Straight and strong. That fence will outlast me. Thank you.
A fine fence. Even the neighbour said so. Grudgingly.
Still leaning, but less. I'll take less.
Not finished. We'll prop it for now. Thank you for trying.
Fence mended. No neighbour complaints filed. A miracle. Logged.
{client} says the fence is straight and the neighbours are still talking to each other. Nice work.
{neighbour} says the fence has always stood a hand's width too far onto their side. Always.
This post crumbles like a biscuit when you touch it. Termites. The old posts are hollow.
{client} and {neighbour} both want the line their way. Split it fair, or side with one of them?
Patch the Roof Before the Rain
{client}'s roof at {roof} is leaking and the rain's due tonight. Tiles from {yard}. {pay}.
The leak is right over the futon. Of course it is. Fresh tiles from {yard}, and seal the joins.
Every tile overlaps the one below. Like fish scales. Get it backwards and it's a waterfall.
Good. Ladder's round the side. Or do you just walk up walls?
Thank you. Watch the ridge, it's slippery with moss.
Then it's buckets on the floor again tonight.
No? I'll move the futon. Again. It's practically on wheels.
How many tiles left? The clouds are coming in.
I can hear you up there. Is that hammering, or falling?
Not a drip. Not one. I'll sleep dry for the first time in a month.
The whole roof's sound. Listen to the rain. Isn't it lovely when it's outside?
The rain beat us to it. Buckets out, everyone.
Still leaking, but slower. I'll take slower.
Roof repaired. You're damp at the edges. Close call, was it? Logged.
{client} says the house stayed dry all night. Paid in full.
A swallow has built its nest right over the leak. With eggs in it. Move it, very carefully.
The neighbour's cat followed you up the ladder and won't come down. It's yowling at the gutter.
First drops, right on time, and four tiles still to go. Faster!
Haul the Morning Catch
The fish stall's supplier needs a squad at {boat} at dawn to land the catch and carry it to {stall}. {pay}.
Nets out at first light from {boat}. Pull together, all of you, on my count. Then the baskets to {stall}.
The river's cold at dawn. Wear something you don't mind smelling of fish forever.
Good. Dawn means dawn, not after breakfast.
Here's a pair of gloves. Your hands will thank me by the third net.
Then it's a small catch and a short day. The stall won't be pleased.
No? I'll ask the ferryman's kids. They pull hard for a rice ball.
Heave! Heave! Keep the line even.
That's a good basket. Silver all the way down.
Best catch this month. The stall will be sold out by noon.
Full baskets and nobody fell in. That's a good morning on the river.
A thin catch. The fish weren't biting, or we weren't pulling. Either way.
Not much in the nets today. The river gives what it gives.
Fishing haul, done. Please don't stand so close to the desk. Logged.
{client} says the stall sold out before noon. That's your work.
The line just went tight enough to sing. Something enormous has taken it. Hold on!
A rip in the net, right down the middle, and half the catch is slipping out!
River Cleanup Below the Bridge
The river below the market bridge is a mess. {client} wants it cleared from {bank}. Nets and sacks provided. {pay}.
Broken baskets, old sandals, a whole cartwheel. It's all caught below the bridge at {bank}. Fish it out.
The fish won't come back till the water's clean. Neither will my customers.
Good. Here's a net on a pole. Long reach. You'll need it.
Thank you. Sacks by the steps. Rubbish in, fish out.
Fine. The river will carry it off eventually. To the next village.
No? I'll keep picking at it on my days off.
Is that a teapot? Who throws a teapot in a river?
The water's clearing already. I can see the stones.
The river's clean and running clear. The fish will be back by spring.
Look at that. I can see the bottom. I haven't seen the bottom in years.
Still a mess. Never mind. The river forgives slowly.
Some of it's out. Not enough, but some.
River cleanup, done. You've brought half of it back with you on your sandals. Logged.
{client} says the water's running clear under the bridge. Good work.
A corked bottle with a letter inside, addressed to {addressee}. Here, in the village.
A fisher's net is caught on the weir, torn and tangled. Someone's lost a week's work.
The worst of it is caught out in the middle. No net reaches that far. Only water-walking will.
Rake the Park by the Academy
{client} wants the leaves raked in {park} by the Academy. Big piles, no jumping in them. Well. Minimal jumping. {pay}.
Every leaf in {park} in a pile by the shed. The paths first, then the grass. Then the paths again.
Rake with the wind, not against it. The wind does half the work if you let it.
Good. Rakes by the shed. Pick one with all its teeth.
Thank you. If the Academy children help, accept it. Don't expect much.
They'll fall again tomorrow anyway. Leaves are patient.
No? Then the paths stay slippery for another week.
That's a fine pile. Don't. Don't you dare jump in it.
The wind's turning. Rake faster before it undoes you.
Paths clear, grass clear, one great pile. The park looks ready for winter.
Lovely work. The Academy teachers will think it's a different park.
Leaves everywhere still. The wind won. It usually does in autumn.
Not done, but the paths are passable. That's the important part.
Leaf raking, done. There's a leaf in your hair. Two. Logged anyway.
{client} says the park's spotless. For about a day. Autumn, you know.
Under the leaves, a purse. Damp, heavy, and lost weeks ago by the look of it.
{client} is eyeing the pile. Says it's perfect for roasting sweet potatoes, and has brought some.
A lost purse, full of coins. Hand it in so its owner can claim it, or keep what you found?
Snow Off the Roofs and Lanes
Heavy snow on the roofs at {roofs} and the lane at {lane}. Clear it before something gives way. {pay}.
Roofs first. The snow's heavy and wet, and these old beams weren't built for it. Then shovel {lane}.
Push it off the eaves, not onto the path. People have to walk under there.
Good. Shovels by the door. Wrap up warm, it bites up there.
Thank you. There's hot ginger tea when you come down. Lots of it.
Then I'll listen to the beams creak all night. Lovely.
No? We'll shovel ourselves, slowly. And complain loudly.
One roof clear. Hear the beams sigh? That's relief.
The lane's half dug. Watch the ice under the snow.
Every roof clear and the lane open. The whole street can breathe.
Not a single beam cracked. You've saved a lot of winter worry.
Snow still on half the roofs. We'll keep an ear on the beams tonight.
Not clear yet. More snow's coming anyway. We'll go again.
Snow clearing, done. Your nose is the colour of a festival lantern. Logged. Go and get warm.
{client} says the lane's open. The children are already making it slippery again.
A low groan from the roof and the whole sheet of snow is letting go at once. Move!
A snowball, right in the back of the neck. Then three more. {kids} have declared war.
Wedding Flowers, Yamanaka Shop
The Yamanaka flower shop at {shop} has a wedding order to fill and carry to {venue}. {client} will explain. {pay}.
Every flower says something. This order should say "joy", "long life" and "together". Not "farewell".
Pick from the list, wrap them in the white paper, and carry them to {venue}. Not in the sun.
Lovely. Here's the list, and a chart of what each flower means. Study it.
Thank you. Cut the stems on a slant. They drink better.
That's all right. I'll stay late. Flowers don't keep office hours.
No? My aunt will come in. She'll lecture me about it, but she'll come.
Is that a chrysanthemum? Not for a wedding. Back on the shelf.
The bouquets look lovely. Keep them out of the window.
Every flower right and every bouquet fresh. The couple will never know how close it was.
Perfect. You've an eye for this. If you ever leave the shinobi life, there's a job here.
Wilted and wrong. Well. The couple will be too happy to notice. I hope.
Not what they ordered. I'll go and apologise myself.
Wedding flowers delivered. You smell lovely, for once. Logged.
{client} says every bouquet said the right thing. I have no idea what that means, but well done.
Look at the chart. Half of this order says "farewell" in the language of flowers. At a wedding.
The heat's getting to them. Petals drooping already. They need to be at {venue} now, not later.
Mind a Stall on Market Day
{client} has to see a supplier and needs someone to mind {stall} on Market Day. Prices are on the tags. {pay}.
Prices on the tags, no discounts, money in the tin. Smile. It's half the sale.
Back by the afternoon bell. If anyone asks for credit, the answer is a polite no.
Good. The tin's under the cloth. Count it now, count it later.
Thank you! Don't let the old woman with the green shawl talk you down. She tries every week.
Then I'll shut the stall and lose a morning's sales. Terrific.
No? I'll ask the stall next door. They'll pocket every third coin.
Selling well? Good. Keep the fresh ones at the front.
That's a lot of coins in the tin. You're a natural.
Look at the tin! You sold more than I do. Should I be worried?
Every coin accounted for and the shelves half empty. Wonderful.
The tin's light and the shelf's still full. A slow day. It happens.
Not a good day for the stall. Never mind. Market Day comes again.
Stall minded, takings counted. {client} says you've got a merchant's tongue. Logged.
Market stall job, done. Did you buy anything? Everyone buys something.
Here comes the most famous haggler in the market, pointing at the best piece, offering half.
Small hands, quick feet, and the purse that was on the counter is gone. {thief} is running!
A festival crowd, all at once, every hand waving coins. Serve fast and count faster.
The haggler won't budge and won't leave. Hold the price on the tag, or give in and sell it cheap?
Sweep the Shrine, Retie the Charms
The shrine needs its steps swept at {steps} and the weathered charms retied. {client} will show you how. {pay}.
Sweep from the top down, always. Then the charms on the rack, fresh cord, the old knots undone with care.
Every charm is someone's wish. Treat each one like it matters. It does, to them.
Thank you. The broom's by the gate. Bow before you start. It's polite.
Good. The cord is in the basket. Double knot, then tuck the end.
The steps will wait. They've been waiting for centuries.
No? The wishes will just have to hang on a little longer.
Top half swept. Don't hurry the bottom steps. They're the oldest.
Neat knots. The charms will hold through winter now.
The steps are clean and the charms are fresh. The shrine looks cared for again.
Lovely, careful work. The gods notice that sort of thing. So do I.
Half done. The shrine is patient. We'll finish another day.
Not finished, but no harm. Come back when you can.
Shrine cleaning, logged. Did you make a wish while you were up there? Everyone does.
{client} sends thanks and a small charm for the squad. It's for safe roads, apparently.
The offerings keep vanishing. The crows are taking them, and the roof at {crow_roost} is their hoard.
Fried tofu at the fox statue again, fresh this morning. The priest wants to know who leaves it.
Training Ground Upkeep
{ground} needs its dummies and posts repaired and the field raked. {client} has the tools. {pay}.
New straw in the dummies, rope on the posts, then rake the field smooth. Every squad in the Leaf uses this ground.
Leave it better than you found it. That's the only rule on a training ground.
Good. Straw's in the shed, rope's on the hook.
Right. Start with the post that's leaning. It's been bothering me for a month.
Then the next squad trains on broken posts. They'll survive.
No? I'll patch what I can before the morning classes.
That dummy's fatter than it was. Too much straw? No, it's fine. Firm.
Half the field raked. Keep your lines straight.
Posts straight, dummies stuffed, field smooth. Best it's looked all season.
Good work. Every squad that trains here tomorrow owes you one.
Still a few broken posts. Squads will just have to aim around them.
Not finished. I'll do the rest at dawn. Thank you anyway.
Training ground upkeep, done. Somebody will break it all again by Friday. Logged.
{client} says the field's never been flatter. Paid.
Ow. The grass is full of shuriken. Last week's class never picked them up.
{challenger} from another squad is waiting by the post with a grin. Wants a spar before you go.
